questions.stem: A wire of length $l$ is in the form of a circular loop A of one turn. This loop is reshaped into loop B of three turns. Find the ratio of the magnetic fields at the centres of loop A and loop B for the same current through them.
questions.solution:
For loop A: $B_1 = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2r}$
When the loop has one turn, $2\pi r = l \Rightarrow r = \frac{l}{2\pi}$
Similarly for loop B: $B_2 = \frac{\mu_0 3I}{2r'}$
When the loop has 3 turns, $3 \times 2\pi r' = l \Rightarrow r' = \frac{l}{6\pi}$
Then, $\frac{B_1}{B_2} = \frac{\frac{\mu_0 I}{2r}}{\frac{\mu_0 3I}{2r'}} = \frac{1}{3}\frac{r'}{r}$
Replacing the values of $r'$ and $r$ in terms of $l$:
$\frac{B_1}{B_2} = \frac{1}{3} \times \frac{l/6\pi}{l/2\pi} = \frac{1}{9}$

questions.stem: What is meant by the term 'displacement current'? Briefly explain how this current is different from a conduction current.
questions.solution:
Displacement current is the current which comes into existence due to the rate of change of electric flux with respect to time, then,
$$I_d = \epsilon_0 \frac{d\phi_E}{dt}$$
Conduction current:
(i) $I_c = \frac{dq}{dt}$
(ii) Due to flow of net charges
Displacement current:
(i) $I_d = \epsilon_0 \frac{d\phi_E}{dt}$
(ii) Due to change in electric field with respect to time [Changing in flux w.r.t. time]

questions.stem: State Huygens principle. How did Huygens explained the absence of the backwave?
questions.solution:
Huygens principle states that, every point on a given wave front may be considered as a new source of secondary wavelets which spread out with the speed of light (vacuum) in that medium and the new wave front is the forward envelope of the secondary wavelets at that instant.
Huygens said that the amplitude of the secondary wavelets is maximum in the forward direction and zero in the backward direction, using this adhoc assumption, Huygens explained the absence of the backwave.

questions.stem: The refractive indices of two media A and B are $2$ and $\sqrt{2}$ respectively. What is the critical angle for their interface?
questions.solution:
Given: $\mu_A = 2$ and $\mu_B = \sqrt{2}$
For critical angle light should be travelled from medium A to medium B. Then from Snell's law
$\sin i_c = \frac{1}{\mu_{AB}} = \frac{\mu_B}{\mu_A} = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}$
$i_c = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\right) = 45^\circ$

questions.or_stem: Using Bohr's postulates, obtain the expression for radius of $n^{\mathrm{th}}$ stable orbit in a hydrogen atom.
questions.or_solution:
The electrostatic attraction force between electron and nucleus provided a necessary centripetal force for revolving electron in a circular path. i.e.
$$\frac{kZe^{2}}{r_n^{2}} = \frac{mv_n^{2}}{r_n}$$
$$v_n^{2} = \frac{kZe^{2}}{mr_n} \qquad \ldots(1)$$
Then, from Bohr's second postulate
$$mv_n r_n = \frac{nh}{2\pi}$$
$$\Rightarrow v_n = \frac{nh}{2\pi m r_n} \qquad \ldots(2)$$
From equation (1) and (2)
$$\frac{n^{2}h^{2}}{4\pi^{2}m^{2}r_n^{2}} = \frac{kZe^{2}}{mr_n}$$
$$r_n = \left(\frac{h^{2}}{4\pi^{2}e^{2}km}\right)\frac{n^{2}}{Z}$$
Put the value $\pi$, $k$, $h$, $m$, $e$. Then we get
$$r_n = 0.529 \times 10^{-8} \times \frac{n^{2}}{Z}\ \mathrm{cm}$$
$$r_n = 0.529 \times n^{2}\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}} \qquad [\text{For hydrogen } Z = 1]$$

questions.stem: Explain the roles of diffusion current and drift current in the formation of the depletion layer in a p-n junction diode.
questions.solution: During the formation of pn-junction, due to the concentration gradient across p and n sides, holes diffuse from p side to n-side and electrons diffuses from n-side to p-side. This motion of charge carrier gives rise to diffusion current across the junction and initially its value is much heigher. Due to diffusion current a layer of positive charge on n-side and a layer of negative charge on p-side junction are developed. This space-charge region on either side of the junction together is known as depletion region. Due to this region an electric field is developed at the junction. Due to this field an electron moves from p-side of the junction to n-side and a hole of the junction moves from n-side to p-side. The motion of charge carriers due to the electric field is called drift. Initially drift current value is lower. After some instant of time diffusion current is equal to drift current p-n junction is formed.

questions.stem: A potential difference $V$ is applied across a conductor of length $\ell$ and uniform cross-section area $A$. How will the (i) electric field $E$, (ii) drift velocity $v_d$, and (iii) current density $j$ be affected when (a) $V$ is doubled and (b) $\ell$ is halved (keeping other factors constant) ?
questions.solution:
(a) When $V$ is doubled
(i) $E$ is doubled due to $E = \frac{V}{\ell}$ & $E' = \frac{2V}{\ell} = 2E$
(ii) $v_d$ is doubled due to $v_d = \frac{e\tau V}{m\ell}$ & $v_d' = \frac{e\tau 2V}{m\ell} = 2v_d$
(iii) $J$ is doubled due to $J = \frac{ne^{2}\tau V}{m\ell}$ & $J' = \frac{ne^{2}\tau 2V}{m\ell} = 2J$
(b) When $\ell$ is half.
(i) $E$ is doubled due to $E = \frac{V}{\ell}$ & $E' = \frac{V}{\ell/2} = 2E$
(ii) $v_d$ is doubled due to $v_d = \frac{e\tau V}{m\ell}$ & $v_d' = \frac{e\tau V}{m\frac{\ell}{2}} = 2v_d$
(iii) $J$ is doubled due to $J = \frac{ne^{2}\tau V}{m\ell}$ & $J' = \frac{ne^{2}\tau V}{m\frac{\ell}{2}} = 2J$

questions.stem: What is meant by the term 'mutual inductance' of a pair of coils? Obtain an expression for the mutual inductance of two long coaxial solenoids, each of length $l$ but having different number of turns $N_1$ and $N_2$ and radii $r_1$ and $r_2$ ($r_2 > r_1$).
questions.solution:
Mutual inductance of coil is numerically equal to the magnetic flux liked with the secondary coil, produced by unit current flowing through the primary coil.
For I coil, $\phi_1 = M_{12} I_2 \qquad ...(1)$
where $\phi_1$ is the flux through I coil.
Similarly,
$\phi_1 = (B_2 \cdot A_1)N_1 = B_2 A_1 N_1\ [\because \vec{B}_2 \parallel \vec{A}_1]$
$= \left(\frac{\mu_0 N_2 I_2}{\ell}\right) A_1 N_1$
$= \frac{\mu_0 N_1 N_2 A_1 I_2}{\ell} \qquad ...(2)$
From (1) & (2)
$M_{12} I_2 = \frac{\mu_0 N_1 N_2 A_1 I_2}{\ell}$
$\Rightarrow M_{12} = \frac{\mu_0 N_1 N_2 A_1}{\ell}$

questions.stem: An ac source $v = v_m \sin \omega t$ is connected across an ideal capacitor. Derive the expression for the (i) current flowing in the circuit, and (ii) reactance of the capacitor. Plot a graph of current $i$ versus $\omega t$.
questions.solution:
(i) Applying KVL in this circuit
$V = V_C$
$V_o \sin \omega t = \frac{q}{C} \qquad [\because q = CV_c]$
$\Rightarrow q = CV_0 \sin \omega t$
Differentiating w.r.t. time then
$\frac{dq}{dt} = \frac{d}{dt}(CV_o \sin \omega t) = CV_o \frac{d}{dt}(\sin \omega t)$
$I = V_o C\omega \cos \omega t \Rightarrow I = \frac{V_o}{1/\omega C} \cos \omega t$
$I = \frac{V_o}{X_c} \cos \omega t \qquad \left\{\because X_c = \frac{1}{\omega C}\right\}$
$I = I_o \cos \omega t = I_o \sin\left(\omega t + \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \qquad \left\{\because I_o = \frac{V_o}{X_c}\right\}$
Compare this equation with $V = V_o \sin \omega t$
Thus current is leading the voltage by an angle $\frac{\pi}{2}$.
(ii) Reactance of the capacitor is $X_c = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{2\pi \nu C} \qquad \left\{\because X_c \propto \frac{1}{\nu}\right\}$
Graph of current $I$ versus $\omega t$: see figure.
questions.or_stem: A series combination of an inductor $L$, a capacitor $C$ and a resistor $R$ is connected across an ac source of voltage in a circuit. Obtain an expression for the average power consumed by the circuit. Find power factor for (i) purely inductive circuit, and (ii) purely resistive circuit.
questions.or_solution:
When a voltage $V = V_m \sin \omega t$ applied to a series LCR circuit then a current in the circuit given by $I = i_m \sin(\omega t + \phi)$. Then instantaneous power $P$ supplied by the source is
$P = V i = V_m \sin \omega t \times i_m \sin(\omega t + \phi)$
$P = V_m i_m \sin \omega t \times \sin(\omega t + \phi)$
$\Rightarrow P = \frac{V_m i_m}{2}\left\{2 \sin \omega t \sin(\omega t + \phi)\right\}$
$\Rightarrow P = \frac{V_m i_m}{2}\left\{\cos(\omega t - \omega t - \phi) - \cos(\omega t + \omega t + \phi)\right\}$
$\{\because 2 \sin A \sin B = \cos(A-B) - \cos(A+B)\}$
$\Rightarrow P = \frac{V_m i_m}{2}\left\{\cos\phi - \cos(2\omega t + \phi)\right\}$
For average power, the second term becomes zero for a complete cycle then,
$P_{av} = \frac{V_m i_m}{2}\cos\phi = \frac{V_m}{\sqrt{2}}\frac{i_m}{\sqrt{2}}\cos\phi$
$\Rightarrow P_{av} = V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos\phi$
Where $\phi$ is the phase difference between voltage & current.
(i) For purely inductive circuit $P_{avg} = 0$
or $V_{rms} I_{rms} \cos\phi = 0$
or Power factor $\cos\phi = 0$
(ii) For purely resistive circuit phase angle $\phi = 0$; then
$P_{av} = V_{rms} I_{rms} (\cos\phi) = V_{rms} I_{rms} = P_{max}$
So, $\cos\phi = 1$

questions.stem: Calculate the wavelength of de Broglie waves associated with a proton having $\left(\frac{500}{1.673}\right)\ \mathrm{eV}$ energy. How will the wavelength be affected for an $\alpha$-particle having the same energy?
questions.solution:
Energy of proton $= \frac{500}{1.673}\ \mathrm{eV} = \frac{500}{1.673} \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J} = 47.82 \times 10^{-18}\ \mathrm{J}$
de-Broglie wavelength of proton $\lambda_p = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2m_p E_k}}$
$\lambda_p = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{\sqrt{2 \times 1.67 \times 10^{-27} \times 47.82 \times 10^{-18}}} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{\sqrt{1.59.72 \times 10^{-45}}} = \frac{6.63 \times 10^{-34}}{3.996 \times 10^{-22}} = 1.659 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$
$\simeq 1.7 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$
de-Broglie wavelength of $\alpha$-particle having the same energy is, $\lambda_\alpha$
$\lambda_\alpha = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2m_\alpha E_k}} = \frac{h}{\sqrt{2(4m_p)E_k}} \qquad \{\because m_\alpha = 4m_p\}$
$\lambda_\alpha = \frac{\lambda_p}{2} = 0.85 \times 10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m}$
So de Broglie wavelength of $\alpha$-particle is half of $\lambda_p$.

questions.stem:
(i) Prove that the nuclear density is same for all nuclei.
(ii) Draw a plot of potential energy of a pair of nucleons as a function of their separation. Draw two inferences from this plot.
questions.solution:
(i) Density of nucleus $= \frac{\text{Mass of nucleus}}{\text{Volume of nucleus}}$
$\rho = \frac{mA}{\frac{4}{3}\pi R^{3}} \Rightarrow \rho = \frac{3m}{4\pi R_0^{3}} \qquad \{\because R = R_0 A^{1/3}\}$
$\Rightarrow \rho = \frac{A \times 1.66 \times 10^{27}\ \mathrm{kg}}{\frac{4}{3} \times 3.14 \times \left(1.2 \times 10^{-15}\right)^{3} A} \approx 10^{17}\ \mathrm{kg/m^{3}}$
It is clear that the density of nucleus is constant.
(ii) Plot of potential energy versus separation: see figure.
- The potential energy is a minimum at a distance $r_0$ of about $0.8\ \mathrm{fm}$.
- The force is attractive for distances larger than $0.8\ \mathrm{fm}$ and repulsive for distances less than $0.8\ \mathrm{fm}$.
questions.or_stem:
(i) Draw a graph to show the variation of the number of scattered particles detected (N) in Geiger-Marsden experiment as a function of scattering angle ($\theta$).
(ii) Discuss briefly two conclusions that can be drawn from this graph and how they lead to the discovery of nucleus in an atom.
questions.or_solution:
(i) Graph of number of scattered particles detected versus scattering angle: see figure.
According to Rutherford Scattering formula
$$N(\theta) \propto \frac{1}{\sin^{4}\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)}$$
The experimental finding follow this curve as only $0.14$ percent of the incident $\alpha$-particles are scattered by more than $1^\circ$.
(ii) Conclusion:
- The existence of sufficient empty space within the atom explains why most of the $\alpha$-particles go un-deflected. Small angle of scattering is accounted for by the fact that the nucleus occupies only a fraction of the total volume of the atom.
- The whole positive charge of the atom and almost its entire mass is concentrated in a small region of the atom. Rutherford named this region as the nucleus.

questions.stem:
(i) Define electric flux and write its SI unit.
(ii) Use Gauss' law to obtain the expression for the electric field due to a uniformly charged infinite plane sheet.
(iii) A cube of side $L$ is kept in space, as shown in the figure. An electric field $\vec{E} = (Ax + B)\hat{i}\ \frac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{C}}$ exists in the region. Find the net charge enclosed by the cube.
questions.solution:
(i) The electric flux through a given area is proportional to the total number of electric field lines passing perpendicular to it. It is given as
$$\phi = \vec{E}\cdot\vec{A} = EA\cos\theta$$
Electric flux through an area is the dot product of $\vec{E}$ and $\vec{A}$.
The S.I. Unit of 'electric flux' is $\mathrm{N\,m^{2}C^{-1}}$ or V-m.
(ii) Direction of electric field due to uniformly charged infinite plane sheet:
It is clear from fig. that if whole sheet can be assumed to be made of Symmetrically situated area elements, then the resultant field will be directed $\perp$ to the sheet.
Determine the magnitude of electric field:
As shown in figure, considering a cylindrical Gaussian surface of cross section $A$
Flux through curved surface:
$$\phi = \int \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{S} = \int E\,ds\cos 90^\circ = 0 \qquad \{\because \vec{E} \perp d\vec{s}\}$$
Curved surface does not contribute to the flux.
Flux through both end caps:
$$\phi = \oint \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{S} = \oint E\,dS\cos 0^\circ = EA \qquad \{\because \vec{E} \parallel d\vec{s}\}$$
Hence, the total flux through the closed surface is:
$\phi$ = Flux through both end caps + flux through curved surface
$$\phi = EA + EA + 0 = 2EA \qquad (1)$$
Now according to Gauss' law for electrostatics
$$\phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_{0}} \qquad (2)$$
Comparing equations (1) and (2), we get
$$2EA = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_{0}}$$
$$E = \frac{q}{2\varepsilon_{0}A} \qquad (3)$$
$$E = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_{0}} \qquad \left\{\because \sigma = \frac{q}{A}\right\}$$
The electric field is uniform and does not depend on the distance from the uniformly charged plane sheet.
(iii) Since the electric field has only $x$ component for faces other than shaded, the angle between $\vec{E}$ and $\Delta\vec{S}$ is $\pm\frac{\pi}{2}$.
Therefore, the flux $\phi = \vec{E}\cdot\Delta\vec{S}$ is separately zero for each face of the cube except the two shaded ones.
Similarly for right face
The corresponding fluxes through the shaded sides are
$$\phi_{L} = \vec{E}_{L}\cdot\vec{S}_{L} = -BS_{L} \qquad \left[\because \theta = 180^\circ\ \text{and}\ E_{L} = (B)\ \tfrac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{C}}\ (x = 0\ \text{at the left face})\right]$$
$$\phi_{L} = -BL^{2} \qquad \{\because S_{L} = L^{2}\}$$
and
$$\phi_{R} = E_{R}\cdot S_{R} = (AL + B)L^{2} \qquad \left[\because \theta = 0^\circ\ \text{and}\ E_{R} = (AL + B)\ \tfrac{\mathrm{N}}{\mathrm{C}}\ (x = L\ \text{at the right face})\right]$$
Net flux through the cube
$$\phi = \phi_{R} + \phi_{L}$$
$$\phi = AL^{3} + BL^{2} - BL^{2}$$
$$\phi = AL^{3}$$
We can use Gauss' law to find the total charge $q$ inside the cube.
We have $\phi = \frac{q}{\varepsilon_{0}}$ or $q = \phi\varepsilon_{0}$.
Therefore, $q = AL^{3}\varepsilon_{0}$
questions.or_stem:
(i) Define electric potential at a point and write its SI unit.
(ii) Two capacitors are connected in series. Derive an expression of the equivalent capacitance of the combination.
(iii) Two point charges $+q$ and $-q$ are located at points $(3a, 0)$ and $(0, 4a)$ respectively in x-y plane. A third charge $Q$ is kept at the origin. Find the value of $Q$, in terms of $q$ and $a$, so that the electrostatic potential energy of the system is zero.
questions.or_solution:
(i) Electric potential: The amount of work needed to bring a unit positive charge from infinity to a specific point inside the electric field of a positive charge is called electric potential at that point. S.I. unit of electric potential is V (volt).
(ii) Two capacitor of equal capacity $C$ are connected to a potential $V$.
In series combination of capacitors all capacitors have same charge but different potential difference.
$\because C_{s} \Rightarrow$ equivalent Capacitance
Total charge $q = C_{s}V$
Combined (total) potential difference on all capacitors are equal to voltage of battery.
$$V = V_{1} + V_{2}$$
Using $V = \frac{q}{C} \Rightarrow \frac{q}{C_{s}} = \frac{q}{C_{1}} + \frac{q}{C_{2}} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{C_{s}} = \frac{1}{C_{1}} + \frac{1}{C_{2}}$
So equivalent capacitance
$$C_{s} = \frac{C_{1}C_{2}}{C_{1} + C_{2}}$$
(iii) Total electrostatic potential energy of the system
$$U = \frac{kQq}{3a} + \frac{kq(-q)}{5a} + \frac{k(-q)Q}{4a}$$
$$U = \frac{kq}{a}\left(\frac{Q}{3} - \frac{q}{5} - \frac{Q}{4}\right)$$
Given: $U = 0$ then $\frac{kq}{a}\left(\frac{Q}{3} - \frac{q}{5} - \frac{Q}{4}\right) = 0$
But $\frac{kq}{a} \neq 0$, So $\frac{Q}{3} - \frac{q}{5} - \frac{Q}{4} = 0$
$$\Rightarrow \frac{Q}{3} - \frac{Q}{4} = \frac{q}{5} \Rightarrow \frac{4Q - 3Q}{12} = \frac{q}{5}$$
$$\Rightarrow Q = \frac{12}{5} \times q = 2.4\,q$$

questions.stem:
(i) Write the principle and explain the working of a moving coil galvanometer. A galvanometer as such cannot be used to measure the current in a circuit. Why?
(ii) Why is the magnetic field made radial in a moving coil galvanometer? How is it achieved ?
questions.solution:
(i) Principle: When a current carrying coil is placed in a uniform magnetic field, it experience a torque and got deflected. By measuring the amount of deflection, we can measure the current.
Working: Suppose the coil is suspended freely in the uniform magnetic field.
The rectangular coil carrying current $I$ when placed in the magnetic field experience a torque whose magnitude a given by
$$\tau = BINA\sin\theta = BINA \qquad [\because \theta = 90^\circ]$$
Due to deflecting torque, the coil rotates and spiral spring is twisted. A restoring torque is set up in the spiral spring.
Let $\theta$ be the twist produced in the spiral spring due to rotation of coil and $K$ be the restoring torque per unit twist of the spiral spring.
Then, total restoring torque produced $= k\theta$
In equilibrium position of the coil, Deflecting torque = Restoring torque
$$\therefore\ BINA = K\theta$$
$$\Rightarrow I = \frac{K}{BNA}\theta \Rightarrow I = G\theta \qquad \{\text{Where } \theta \text{ is the deflection in the coil}\}$$
Where, $\frac{K}{BNA} = G$ = constant for a galvanometer
Due to following reason galvanometer cannot be used to measure current.
• A galvanometer has a finite large resistance and is connected in series in the circuit, so it will increase the resistance of circuit and hence change the value of current in the circuit.
• A galvanometer is a very sensitive device, it gives full scale deflection for the current of the order of microampere, hence if connected as such it will not measure current of the order of ampere.
(ii) Importance of production of radial magnetic field: In a radial magnetic field, magnetic torque remains maximum for all positions of the coils. It is produced due to cylindrical pole pieces and soft iron core.
questions.or_stem:
(i) Derive an expression for magnetic field on the axis of a current carrying circular loop.
(ii) Write any two points of difference between a diamagnetic and a paramagnetic substance.
questions.or_solution:
(i) Magnetic field on axis of a current carrying loop:
Let current $I$ is flowing through a loop of radius $R$. We want to find magnetic field at an axial point $P$. The angle between each element $d\vec{\ell}$ and $\vec{r}$ is $\theta = 90^\circ$.
Using Biot-savart's law -
$$d\vec{B} = \frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r^{2}}\left(d\vec{\ell}\times\hat{r}\right)$$
Taking the magnitude
$$dB = \frac{\mu_{0}I}{4\pi r^{2}}\,d\ell\sin 90^\circ \qquad \{\because d\vec{\ell} \perp \hat{r}\}$$
$$dB = \frac{\mu_{0}I\,d\ell}{4\pi r^{2}}$$
It is clear that the magnetic field developed at point 'P' due to symmetrical elements each of length $d\ell$ have equal magnitude. The equatorial components $dB\cos\phi$ due to both elements get cancelled while axial components $dB\sin\phi$ get added. In this way the net magnetic field is only because of axial component $dB\sin\phi$.
Magnetic field developed at 'P' due to whole circular loop is given by
$$B_{axis} = \int_{0}^{2\pi R} dB\sin\phi \Rightarrow B_{axis} = \int_{0}^{2\pi R}\frac{\mu_{0}Id\ell}{4\pi r^{2}}\sin\phi \Rightarrow B_{axis} = \frac{\mu_{0}IR}{4\pi r^{3}}\int_{0}^{2\pi R} d\ell$$
From figure: $\sin\phi = R/r$ and $r = (R^{2} + x^{2})^{1/2}$
$$B_{axis} = \frac{\mu_{0}IR}{4\pi r^{3}}\left(2\pi R - 0\right) \Rightarrow B_{axis} = \frac{\mu_{0}IR^{2}}{2r^{3}} \Rightarrow B_{axis} = \frac{\mu_{0}IR^{2}}{2\left(R^{2} + x^{2}\right)^{3/2}}$$
If the coil have $N$ turns then,
$$B_{axis} = \frac{\mu_{0}NIR^{2}}{2\left(R^{2} + x^{2}\right)^{3/2}}$$
The direction of magnetic field is along $x$-axis.
(ii) Difference between diamagnetic and paramagnetic substance.
 | Diamagnetic Substance | Paramagnetic Substance
(1) In an external magnetic field | These substances weakly magnetised in the direction opposite to that of applied field. | These substances weakly magnetised in the same direction of the applied field.
(2) Applying non uniform magnetic field. | It tends to move from the stronger to the weak part of the field. | It tends to move from the weaker to the stronger part of the field.

questions.stem:
(i) Draw a ray diagram showing the formation of a real image of an object placed at a distance 'u' in front of a concave mirror of radius of curvature 'R'. Hence, obtain the relation for the image distance $v$ in terms of $u$ and $R$.
(ii) A $1.8\ \mathrm{m}$ tall person stands in front of a convex lens of focal length $1\ \mathrm{m}$, at a distance of $5\ \mathrm{m}$. Find the position and height of the image formed.
questions.solution:
(i) Relation between $u$, $v$ and $f$ for concave mirror
where $u$ = distance between pole and object, $v$ = distance between pole and image and $f$ = focal length
In $\Delta A'FB'$ and $\Delta RFQ$
$\angle QFR = \angle A'FB'$ and $\angle A'B'F = \angle RQF = 90^\circ$, $\angle B'A'F = \angle FRQ$
i.e., $\Delta A'FB' \sim \Delta RFQ$, then
$$\frac{A'B'}{QR} = \frac{FB'}{QF} \Rightarrow \frac{A'B'}{AB} = \frac{FB'}{QF} \qquad \ldots(1) \qquad \{\text{from figure } QR = AB\}$$
Similarly $\Delta ABC \sim \Delta A'B'C$, hence
$$\frac{A'B'}{AB} = \frac{B'C}{BC} \qquad \ldots(2)$$
From eq. (1) and (2)
$$\frac{FB'}{QF} = \frac{B'C}{BC}$$
Point $Q$ is very close to $P$. Hence $\Rightarrow QF \approx PF$
$$\frac{PB' - PF}{PF} = \frac{PC - PB'}{PB - PC}$$
Applying sign convention $PB' = -v$, $PF = -f$, $PC = -2f$ and $PB = -u$
$$\frac{-v - (-f)}{-f} = \frac{-2f - (-v)}{u - (-2f)} \Rightarrow \frac{-v + f}{-f} = \frac{-2f + v}{-u + 2f}$$
On solving, $uv - uf = vf$
divide by $uvf$
$$\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{u} + \frac{1}{v}$$ (This is mirror's equation).
(ii) Given $h = 1.8\ \mathrm{m}$, focal length of Convex lens $f = 1\ \mathrm{m}$, and $u = -5\ \mathrm{m}$ then $v = ?$ and $h' = ?$
From lens formula $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{1\ \mathrm{m}} = \frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{(-5\ \mathrm{m})} \Rightarrow \frac{1}{v} = \frac{1}{1} - \frac{1}{5} = \frac{4}{5\ \mathrm{m}}$
$v = 1.25\ \mathrm{m}$
Magnification $m = \frac{h'}{h} = \frac{v}{u}$
$$\frac{h'}{1.8\ \mathrm{m}} = \frac{1.25\ \mathrm{m}}{-5\ \mathrm{m}} = -0.25$$
$$\Rightarrow h' = -0.25 \times 1.8\ \mathrm{m}$$
$$\Rightarrow h' = -0.45\ \mathrm{m}$$
questions.or_stem:
(i) Draw a ray diagram showing retraction of a ray of light through a triangular glass prism. Hence, obtain the relation for the refractive index ($\mu$) in terms of angle of prism ($A$) and angle of minimum deviation ($\delta_{m}$).
(ii) The radii of curvature of the two surfaces of a concave lens are $20\ \mathrm{cm}$ each. Find the refractive index of the material of the lens if its power is $-5.0\ \mathrm{D}$.
questions.or_solution:
(i) In quadrilateral $AQNR$
$$A + \angle AQN + \angle QNR + \angle NRA = 360^\circ$$
$$A + \angle QNR = 180^\circ \qquad \ldots(1) \qquad \{\angle AQN = \angle NRA = 90^\circ\}$$
In $\Delta QNR$,
$$r_{1} + r_{2} + \angle QNR = 180^\circ \qquad \ldots(2)$$
From eq. (1) and (2)
$$A = r_{1} + r_{2} \qquad \ldots(3)$$
Angle of deviation ($\delta$)
$$\delta = (i - r_{1}) + (e - r_{2}) \quad \Rightarrow \quad \delta = (i + e) - (r_{1} + r_{2})$$
$$\delta = (i + e) - A \qquad \ldots(4)$$
At minimum deviation, the refracted ray inside the prism becomes parallel to its's base. Hence in case of minimum deviation -
$$i = e,\ r_{1} = r_{2} = r \ \text{and}\ \delta = \delta_{m}$$
From eq. (3)
$$A = 2r \Rightarrow r = A/2 \qquad \ldots(5)$$
From eq. (4)
$$\delta_{m} = 2i - A \Rightarrow i = \frac{\delta_{m} + A}{2} \qquad \ldots(6)$$
From snell's law -
$$_{a}\mu_{g} = \frac{\sin i}{\sin r_{1}} \ \Rightarrow\ \mu = \frac{\sin i}{\sin r} \qquad \{\text{At minimum deviation } r_{1} = r_{2} = r\}$$
$$\mu = \frac{\sin\left(\frac{\delta_{m} + A}{2}\right)}{\sin\left(\frac{A}{2}\right)}$$
This is the prism formula.
(ii) For concave lens given values $R_{1} = -20\ \mathrm{cm}$, $R_{2} = +20\ \mathrm{cm}$, $P = -5.0\ \mathrm{D}$ and $\mu = ?$
From lens maker formula
$$\frac{1}{f} = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{1}{R_{1}} - \frac{1}{R_{2}}\right)$$
$$-\frac{1}{20} = (\mu - 1)\left(-\frac{1}{20} - \frac{1}{20}\right) = (\mu - 1)\left(\frac{-2}{20}\right) \qquad \left\{\because f = \frac{1}{P},\ f = -\frac{100}{5} = -20\ \mathrm{cm}\right\}$$
$$\Rightarrow \mu - 1 = 0.5 \Rightarrow \mu = 1.5$$

questions.stem:
A beam of electrons moving horizontally with a velocity of $3 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m/s}$ enters a region between two plates as shown in the figure. A suitable potential difference is applied across the plates such that the electron beam just strikes the edge of the lower plate.

Answer the following questions based on the above :
(a) How long does an electron take to strike the edge ? (1)
(b) What is the shape of the path followed by the electron and why? (1)
(c) Find the potential difference applied. (2)
OR
(c) Find the magnitude and direction of the magnetic field which should be created in the space between the plates so that the electron beam goes straight un-deflected. (2)
questions.solution:
Velocity of $e^{-}$ beam $= 3 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m/s}$
Assumption $e^{-}$ beam enters through midpoint.
(a) Time taken to strike the edge
$$t = \frac{3 \times 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m}}{3 \times 10^{7}\ \mathrm{m/s}} = 1 \times 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{s} = 1\ \mathrm{ns}$$
(b) Shape of the path is parabolic due to second equation of motion [along-axis]
$$S_{y} = u_{y}t + \frac{1}{2}a_{y}t^{2}$$
In this condition $u_{y} = 0$ then
$$S_{y} = \frac{1}{2}a_{y}t^{2}$$
This equation is similar to equation of parabola.
Parabolic path, due to the accelerated motion in vertical direction due to electric field.
(c) Applied potential difference $V = Ed$.
$$V = \frac{ma_{y}}{q}d$$
$$V = \frac{9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 10^{18}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}} \times 1 \times 10^{-2} \simeq 5.7 \times 10^{4}\ \mathrm{volt}$$
For finding the value of $a_{y}$
$\because F = ma = qE \Rightarrow E = \frac{ma_{y}}{q}$
From 2nd equation of motion
$$S_{y} = u_{y}t + \frac{1}{2}a_{y}t^{2}$$
$$0.5 = \frac{1}{2}a_{y}(10^{-9})^{2}$$
$$\Rightarrow a_{y} = 10^{18}\ \mathrm{m/s^{2}}$$
OR
(c) For the electron beam to be un-deflected and moves straight, the magnetic force acting on the electron beam must be equal to electric force.
So, $qvB = qE \Rightarrow B = \frac{E}{v}$ $\qquad \left\{\because E = \frac{V}{d} = \frac{5.7 \times 10^{4}}{10^{-2}} = 5.7 \times 10^{6}\ \frac{\mathrm{V}}{\mathrm{m}}\right\}$
$$B = \frac{5.7 \times 10^{6}}{3 \times 10^{7}} = 1.9 \times 10^{-1} = 0.19\ \mathrm{T}$$
And the direction of this magnetic field is perpendicular outward to the plane of the plates.
So $\vec{B} = 0.19\hat{k}\ \mathrm{T}$

questions.stem:
Diffraction of light is bending of light around the corners of an object whose size is comparable with the wavelength of light. Diffraction actually defines the limits of ray optics. This limit for optical instruments is set by the wavelength of light. An experimental arrangement is set up to observe the diffraction pattern due to a single slit.

Answer the following questions based on the above :
(a) How will the width of central maximum be affected if the wavelength of light is increased? (1)
(b) Under what condition is the first minimum obtained? (1)
(c) Write two points of difference between interference and diffraction patterns. (2)
OR
(c) Two students are separated by a $7\ \mathrm{m}$ partition wall in a room $10\ \mathrm{m}$ high. If both light and sound waves can bend around obstacles, how is it that the students are unable to see each other even though they can converse easily? (2)
questions.solution:
(a) Width of central maxima $\beta = \frac{2\lambda D}{d}$
If the wavelength of light is increased then fringe width also increase (but $d < \lambda$)
(b) Path difference between extreme diffracted ray's at a point on screen should be $\lambda$.
(c) Interference | Diffraction
(1) It is result of superposition between secondary wavelets coming from two coherent sources. | (1) It is result of superposition between secondary wavelets coming from different parts of the same source slit.
(2) All bright fringes are equally illuminated. | (2) Central fringe is brightest and all other fringes have intensity in-decreasing order.
OR
(c) The size of obstacle is very much larger than wavelength of light therefore there is no any diffraction of light waves that's why the students are unable to see.
While sound wave diffracted easily because obstacle size is comparable to wavelength of sound.
